subject: Mathematics
chapter: Chapter 11: Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry
central_question: How can we locate points in three-dimensional space and use their coordinates to measure distances and solve basic geometric problems?
in_scope_units: Introduction: why a point in space requires three coordinates rather than two.
Coordinate axes and coordinate planes in three-dimensional space: the rectangular coordinate system, origin, signs and eight octants.
Coordinates of a point in space: ordered triplets, locating a point, coordinates on axes and planes, and octant identification.
Distance between two points: derivation and use of the three-dimensional distance formula and distance from the origin.
Applications of distance and coordinates: collinearity, triangle and parallelogram checks, loci defined by distances, and centroid-based problems.
Summary and historical note: key facts and the development of three-dimensional coordinate geometry.
banned_topics: Direction cosines and direction ratios of a line
Equations of lines and planes in space
Section formula as a separate general theorem
Sphere equations beyond the distance-based loci explicitly given in this chapter

known_pitfalls.claim: The coordinate x is the distance of P from the XY-plane.
known_pitfalls.correction: For P(x, y, z), x, y and z are the directed perpendicular distances from the YZ-plane, ZX-plane and XY-plane, respectively.

known_pitfalls.claim: A point in the XY-plane may have any value of z.
known_pitfalls.correction: Every point in the XY-plane has z-coordinate 0 and is of the form (x, y, 0).

known_pitfalls.claim: The octant depends on the magnitudes of x, y and z.
known_pitfalls.correction: The octant is determined only by the signs of x, y and z; their magnitudes do not affect the octant.

known_pitfalls.claim: The distance formula is the sum of coordinate differences.
known_pitfalls.correction: The distance is the square root of the sum of the squares of the three coordinate differences.

known_pitfalls.claim: If three pairwise distances are different, the points cannot be collinear.
known_pitfalls.correction: Three points are collinear when the largest of the three distances equals the sum of the other two, as in NCERT Example 4.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with NCERT Example 1 to identify the missing coordinate of a point lying on a face parallel to a coordinate plane.
Use NCERT Example 2 and Exercise 11.1 Q3 to practise octant identification from coordinate signs.
Use NCERT Example 3 to apply the distance formula directly.
Use NCERT Example 4 and Exercise 11.2 Q2 to test collinearity through distances.
Use NCERT Example 5 and Exercise 11.2 Q3 to classify triangles and verify a parallelogram.
Finish with NCERT Examples 6, 8 and 9 for distance loci and a centroid-based coordinate problem.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter contains Exercise 11.1, Exercise 11.2, and the four-question Miscellaneous Exercise on Chapter 11.
